idiom_name: one stateless service per use case (or per aggregate) + injected ports + explicit unit of work
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one stateless service per use case, or one per aggregate with one method per use case, and give it only the ports that use case needs (repositories, domain services, gateways, clock, id generator) injected at construction. The method accepts a request object, loads the aggregates it needs, tells them or a domain service what to do — never re-implementing domain decisions itself — persists through repositories, publishes what happened and returns a response object. The unit of work is opened at the start of the method and committed exactly once at the end, so the whole use case is atomic; a failure before the commit rolls everything back. Application concerns (authorization, idempotency, input validation, tenant resolution, domain-event dispatch) are handled here and nowhere else.
pitfalls: Wrong move: put balance, authorization or eligibility decisions in the application method; failure: entities become data bags and another caller can bypass the rule; instead: tell the aggregate or Domain Service to decide and keep the service to sequencing.

Wrong move: let a repository call commit after each save; failure: a later failure leaves earlier writes committed; instead: enlist every repository in one use-case-owned unit of work and commit once.

Wrong move: call payment, email or another remote API while the database transaction is open; failure: locks and pooled connections are held across network latency and a remote side effect cannot roll back with the database; instead: record an outbox command and dispatch it after commit.

Wrong move: return an ORM entity or accept one from a controller; failure: persistence and presentation become coupled to domain state and lazy-loading behavior; instead: translate request and response DTOs at the boundary.
Wrong move: publish a domain event before commit; failure: consumers observe an event for state that later rolls back; instead: write an outbox row in the same transaction and relay it after commit.

Wrong move: check idempotency after doing side effects; failure: a retried queue message repeats the business operation; instead: claim the key atomically before work and commit that claim with the state change.
Wrong move: make one per-aggregate service own every verb; failure: its constructor and change surface become a god class; instead: split by cohesive use case as dependencies diverge.

Wrong move: call another application service to reuse orchestration; failure: nested transaction ownership and the real use-case boundary become implicit; instead: extract a domain policy or compose the workflow at one application boundary.

Wrong move: share mutable request state on a service instance; failure: concurrent callers observe each other's data; instead: keep the service stateless and pass request data through method parameters.
